summary: _“(a) Declare that the events set out in Paragraph 2(a) to 2(d) of the Petition as Change in Law event impacting revenues and costs during the Operation Period for which the SPL may be compensated in terms of Article 13 of the PPA;_ _“(a) Declare that the events set out in Paragraph 2(a) to 2(f) of the Petition as Change in Law event impacting revenues and costs during the Operation Period for which the Petitioner be compensated in terms of Article 13 of the PPA.;_ permitted to move an appropriate application seeking amendment of the Petition, the Respondents were granted liberty to file their replies to the said IA. On 13.11.2025, the Respondents were again granted an opportunity to file their replies to the IA and the Amended Petition, if any. However, only the Respondents, HPPC and PSPCL, have filed their replies to the IA within the stipulated time, and submissions made therein have already been noted above. During the hearing on 13.11.2025, the learned counsel for both sides also made detailed submissions in the case, including on the maintainability of this IA. In view of this, the Commission deemed it appropriate to first decide on the maintainability of the IA and accordingly reserved orders therein. Posthearing, the Petitioner also filed written submissions, the contents of which are not repeated here for the sake of brevity. _The Commission may, at any stage of the proceedings in a petition, allow either party to alter or amend its pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be considered appropriate, and all such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real issues in controversy between the parties:_ As per the above provisions, the Commission may allow either party to alter or amend its pleadings, necessary for the purpose of determining the real issues in controversy, in such a manner and on such terms as may be considered appropriate at any stage of proceedings in a Petition. However, no application for amendment is to be allowed after the commencement of the final hearing of the Petition, unless the Commission is of the view that, in spite of due diligence, the party could not have raised the matter before the commencement of the final hearing. 26. Having considered the above legal provisions, we now proceed to examine the contention of the contesting parties. First and foremost, the Respondents, PSPCL and HPPC, have contended that the IA is not maintainable as it seeks to substantially modify and expand the scope of the reliefs originally prayed for in Petition No. 215/MP/2021. In particular, the Petitioner has sought to introduce a new cause of action and, on that basis, has sought unsubstantiated financial claims, unilateral revision of implementation methodology, and in-principle capital expenditure, none of which were part of the original Petition. 33. The next test is whether disallowing the proposed amendment would in fact lead to injustice or lead to multiple litigations. As the proposed amendments only pertain to the Petitioner’s claims of compensation against the asserted Change in Law events in the main Petition, we are of the view that disallowing such amendments would in fact lead to injustice to the Petitioner and multiple rounds of litigation, as the Petitioner would be required to file a fresh Petition seeking the compensation for the Change in Law events asserted in this case. As noted, allowing the proposed amendments would enable us not only to examine the validity of the Change in Law events claimed by the Petitioner, but also the extent of compensation under Article 13 of the PPA. Directing the Petitioner to file a separate Petition to determine the Change in Law compensation would result in piecemeal adjudication, and the Commission has, in several cases, disapproved of such an approach while considering an affected party’s Change in Law 36. We have considered the submissions of the parties. As noted above, by way of the proposed amendment, the Petitioner has only sought to incorporate the change in the manner in which the Petitioner has incurred and/or sought to incur expenditure towards its obligation arising out of the claimed Change in Law events. Moreover, the Petitioner has sought recovery of the additional revenue/operational expenditure as incurred due to these Change in Law events only for the period FY 2023-24 onwards and not for the period prior thereto. Pertinently, for the Change in Law having a recurring impact, the money claims pertaining to the three years from the date of filing of the Petition have been allowed by the Commission in several orders, including in the order dated 23.06.2023 in Petition No. 513/MP/2020 (APMuL v. UHBVNL and Ors.). In the present case also, the compensation claims for revenue/operational expenditure as sought to be incorporated by the proposed amendments pertain to a period within 37. In the light of the above discussion, we are of the view that the proposed amendments sought by the Petitioner through the IA deserve to be allowed, as they are necessary for the purpose of determining the real questions in controversy between the parties and proper adjudication of the case. Accordingly, the amended Petition is taken on record, and all the Respondents are again granted liberty to file their respective replies to the amended Petition within four weeks, if not already done so. The Respondents are at liberty to take all such objections as they may consider appropriate, including objections with regard to limitation and other issues on the merits. It is clarified that, in this order, the Commission has only decided that the amendment sought by the Petitioner/SPL should be allowed. The Commission has not expressed any view on the limitation, maintainability and merit of the Petitioner’s claims in this order, and will decide the same after hearing the parties at the stage of final disposal of the Petition.
